credit:unsplash

If you have ever deployed a frontend app to Vercel and immediately started panicking when pages started showing 404 errors, you are not alone. Many developers, especially those working with React, Vue, or Angular, have gone through the exact same experience. The frustrating part? Most of the time, the app is not broken at all. It just behaves differently in production, and understanding why can save you a lot of time and stress.

## What Really Happens When You Deploy [...] ## Conclusion

Deploying a single-page application can feel like stepping into the unknown, but in most cases, it is not your code that is at fault. It is simply the server needing a small nudge to understand your routing. A single rewrite rule can turn hours of frustration into a moment of relief.

Remember this: when your Vercel app shows 404s but works perfectly in development, it is not broken. It just needs a little guidance, and with this simple fix, your app will behave exactly as it should.

2 following [...] ## What Really Happens When You Deploy

When you are developing your app locally, your single-page application uses client-side routing. This means that navigation between pages like `/about`, `/contact`, or `/dashboard/settings` is handled entirely by your frontend code, not the server. Your development server automatically serves `index.html` for all these routes so that your JavaScript router can take over.

In production, however, things are different. When you deploy to Vercel and someone visits `/about` directly, Vercel looks for a file called `/about/index.html`. Since that file does not exist, Vercel returns a 404 error. Suddenly, your app looks like it is broken. And that is when the panic starts.
